correctness.rationale: The path edge vectors form a basis of the zero-sum hyperplane, so every facet is indexed by one sign choice from each opposite vertex pair. The unique facet normal has consecutive differences equal to those signs. The zero-sum variance identity converts its squared norm into the sum of squared signed interval sums. Bounding each interval sum by its length gives the exact maximum \(n(n^2-1)/12\), and equality is forced to the two constant sign patterns. Those opposite facets bound every translated inscribed ball, proving the global inradius. Strict slack at every other facet around the origin proves that the full incenter set has affine dimension \(n-2\). Finally, opposite vertex pairs give an exact lower certificate for the unique minimum enclosing sphere.

value.rationale: Paths are the canonical tree family and their symmetric edge polytopes simultaneously sit in lattice-polytope, finite-metric, and transport geometry. Although the polytope is abstractly a crosspolytope, its standard simple-root realization is strongly nonregular. The theorem identifies a structural metric effect rather than a small numerical refinement: only two facets control the centered maximal inball, the optimal center is nonunique in an entire codimension-one family, every primal vertex controls the unique outer sphere, and the exact radius ratio grows as a cubic square root in the path size. This complements the existing face-number, triangulation, and arithmetic theory with a complete Euclidean ball profile for the fundamental path family.
